analysis.analysis: Our approach exhibits consistently high detection performance across all the generative models, achieving an absolute average improvement of 5.5% over the second best method. On the other hand, almost all competitors successfully distinguish AI-generated images from specific generators, in some cases even achieving near-perfect performance, they completely fail to others. This highlights the inability of those detectors that learn to capture specific types of artifacts to generalize to generators that introduce different types of inconsistencies.

considerations.ethical_risks: False Positives: Suppression of truthful content, potential damage to credibility, censorship, or wrongful accusations. False Negatives: Spread of disinformation, fraud, manipulation of public opinion, or malicious impersonation. Arms Race with Generators: Detection efforts may unintentionally accelerate the realism of harmful generative models.
considerations.factors: The model fails to detect AI-generated images that appear as parts of screenshots, memes, or even in photographs of computer screens and in printed material. This intermediate medium distorts the spectral distribution of the AI-generated image signal and thus, the subtle inconsistencies introduced by the generative approaches become indistinguishable. Also, compression algorithms discard useful information that the model rely on which dramatically drops the performance.
considerations.hardware: The code originally targeted Nvidia L40S 48GB GPU, however many recent cuda-enabled GPUs should be supported. Inference should be effortless performed with less than 8GB of GPU RAM. As training originally targeted a 48GB GPU, a suitable GPU should be presented to reproduce the paper's setup without further modifications of the code.
considerations.inputs_outputs: Input: a directory where the input images are located, Output: a directory where a csv file with the predictions will be written
considerations.instructions:
conda create -n spai python=3.11
conda activate spai
conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio pytorch-cuda=12.4 -c pytorch -c nvidia
pip install -r requirements.txt
Furthermore, the installation of Nvidia APEX is required for training.
The trained weights checkpoint can be downloaded here and should be placed under the weights directory, located under the project's root directory.
To compute the predicted scores for a set of images, place them under a directory and use the following command.
python -m spai --input --output

eval_set.datasets:
AI generated: Glide, Stable Diffusion 1.3 (SD1.3), Stable Diffusion 1.4 (SD1.4), DALLE-2, Stable Diffusion 2 (SD2), Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL), Firefly ref., Flux, Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3), GigaGAN, Midjourney-v5(MJv5), DALLE3 ref., Midjourney-v6.1 (MJv6.1).
Real images: RAISE, FODB, ImageNet, COCO, Open Images.
eval_set.motivation:
To evaluate generalization, we collect a representative sample of 1,000 images from each of several major generative models from ref.. These include early diffusion-based text-to-image models such as Glide, Stable Diffusion 1.3 (SD1.3), and Stable Diffusion 1.4 (SD1.4), which mostly produce images under 0.5 megapixels. We also include samples from more recent diffusion models such as DALLE-2, Stable Diffusion 2 (SD2), and Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL), as well as images from Flux, Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3), and GigaGAN. These approaches represent a group of recent methods, capable of producing images up to 1 megapixel. Finally, we collect images for Midjourney-v5(MJv5), DALLE3 (ref.) and Firefly from ref., as well as for Midjourney-v6.1 (MJv6.1) from ref (631 images).
Regarding the real images, we employ 1k samples from each of RAISE and FODB, as representative sources of images captured by DSLR cameras and smartphones respectively. We include another 1k images from the test sets of ImageNet, COCO, and Open Images that represent a general collection of online images, an object-focused database, and a collection of high-resolution Web images respectively.
eval_set.update: The evaluation set contains both older and state-of-the-art generative methods

model.author: CERTH - The Centre for Research & Technology, Hellas
model.name: SPAI
model.overview: SPAI employs spectral learning to learn the spectral distribution of real images under a self-supervised setup. Then, using the spectral reconstruction similarity it detects AI-generated images as out-of-distribution samples of this learned model. Moreover, it introduces spectral context attention, which enables to efficiently capture subtle spectral inconsistencies in images of any resolution.

training_set.datasets: Following prior work, we train our approach using 180,000 low-resolution (256×256) images generated by a single latent diffusion model introduced by Rombach et al. along with 180,000 real images introduced by Corvi et al.. This balanced dataset allows the model to learn to distinguish between synthetic and real content.
training_set.motivation: The model is trained end-to-end using binary cross-entropy loss between predicted outputs (ŷ) and ground-truth labels (y). Training runs for 35 epochs with the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 5e−4, cosine decay, and 5 epochs of linear warmup. We use a batch size of 72. To enable single-stage training (including the SCA module) without being constrained by image size or patch layout, we generate a fixed number of patches (Ktraining=4) per image using random augmentations. This allows the use of any image for training and ensures an efficient pipeline. At inference time, we use the actual number of patches present in each image. The network uses an embedding dimension D=1024, and each patch is sized at 224×224 pixels. The patch feature dimension is set to Dh=1536. For spectral representation, we use a ViT-B/16 backbone pretrained on ImageNet, following the masked modeling setup of Xie et al., with a masking radius r=16. The ViT has 12 transformer blocks (N=12) and a latent dimension d=768. The backbone’s weights are kept frozen during training while the remaining modules—SRS, SCV, and SCA—are optimized. Training is performed on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU with 48 GB of memory.
training_set.pre_processing: We apply a range of augmentations during training, including random resizing, cropping, rotation, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, and JPEG compression.
